title: Back to School: We Are All Teachers of Language September 1, 2026
author: Andrew Ellison
source: Classical Ed (classicaled.substack.com), adapted from a keynote to Great Hearts Arizona,
summary: In a keynote address to Great Hearts Arizona, Ellison argues that every teacher, regardless of subject, is a teacher of language, because all formal education happens in and through words. He works through discipline after discipline — mathematics, history, the sciences, the arts — showing that even a Euclid proof or a lab report depends on the classical Trivium's arts of grammar, logic, and rhetoric, since language is not just a vehicle for content but 'a co-subject,' the substrate on which every other discipline is built. He closes with a sweeping historical claim that civilizational flourishing and the flourishing of language have always moved together — citing Periclean Athens, the American founding, and the oratory of Churchill and King — and warns that when language grows flat and jargon-ridden, cultures stagnate and become vulnerable to those who use language skillfully for deception.
points: Ellison's central claim reframes the Trivium as universal infrastructure: grammar, logic, and rhetoric underlie every discipline, so a math or science teacher is teaching language just as surely as an English teacher is.

He distinguishes teaching the 'content' of a story from teaching the language in which human experience is rendered, warning that heavy-handed moralizing about a text's 'message' can ruin what literature actually teaches.

His historical argument links eras of civilizational achievement directly to eras of linguistic flourishing — Periclean Athens, Roman statecraft, the American founding, the oratory of Churchill and King — arguing the two have never been separable.

The essay closes with an explicit warning drawn from Confucius: when language is used incorrectly, what is said is not what is meant, and people are left in helpless confusion, vulnerable to demagogues who wield language skillfully to deceive.
quotes: We all teach language, sometimes explicitly and analytically, always implicitly and informally. For all formal education is conducted in and through words, through language.

Our language is not just a means of “content delivery”—it is always a co-subject, the background and scenery, the substrate, the foundation upon which the structure of the arts and sciences is built, even as other academic and intellectual and moral and aesthetic topics appear to be the sole concern.
In teaching literature, we are teaching language about characters and actions and dramatic choices and the detailed, subtle texture of existence as perceived through the human senses.

When language is strong, beautiful, clear, and used to reveal the true and move hearts to right actions and hard choices, human beings accomplish great deeds. Worthy works are wrought. Cultures rise to new heights.
As Confucius puts it in the Analects, “…when language is used incorrectly, what is said is not what is meant, what should be done is left undone…and the people stand around in helpless confusion.
